claim: Plant receptor kinases (RKs) transmembrane signaling has long been thought to involve reciprocal trans-phosphorylation of their intracellular kinase domains.
source: Transmembrane signaling by plant receptor kinases (RKs) has long been thought to involve reciprocal trans-phosphorylation of their intracellular kinase domains.
evidence: This is a statement about the historical understanding in the field, presented as established knowledge.

claim: Many plant receptor kinases have pseudokinase domains.
source: The fact that many of these are pseudokinase domains, however, suggests that additional mechanisms must govern RK signaling activation.
evidence: This is stated as a fact in the manuscript.

claim: Additional mechanisms beyond reciprocal trans-phosphorylation must govern RK signaling activation.
source: The fact that many of these are pseudokinase domains, however, suggests that additional mechanisms must govern RK signaling activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of pseudokinase domains.

claim: Non-catalytic signaling mechanisms of protein kinase domains have been described in metazoans.
source: Non-catalytic signaling mechanisms of protein kinase domains have been described in metazoans, but information is scarce for plants.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from the literature.

claim: Information about non-catalytic signaling mechanisms is scarce for plants.
source: Non-catalytic signaling mechanisms of protein kinase domains have been described in metazoans, but information is scarce for plants.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: A non-catalytic function was recently reported for EFR.
source: Recently, a non-catalytic function was reported for the leucine-rich repeat (LRR)-RK subfamily XIIa member EFR (elongation factor Tu receptor) and phosphorylation-dependent conformational changes were proposed to regulate signaling of RKs with non-RD kinase domains.
evidence: This references recent findings in the literature.

claim: Phosphorylation-dependent conformational changes were proposed to regulate signaling of RKs with non-RD kinase domains.
source: Recently, a non-catalytic function was reported for the leucine-rich repeat (LRR)-RK subfamily XIIa member EFR (elongation factor Tu receptor) and phosphorylation-dependent conformational changes were proposed to regulate signaling of RKs with non-RD kinase domains.
evidence: This references a hypothesis from recent literature.

claim: EFR is an active kinase.
source: EFR is an active kinase, but a kinase-dead variant retains the ability to enhance catalytic activity of its co-receptor kinase BAK1/SERK3 (brassinosteroid insensitive 1-associated kinase 1/somatic embryogenesis receptor kinase 3).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claim: A kinase-dead variant of EFR retains the ability to enhance catalytic activity of BAK1.
source: EFR is an active kinase, but a kinase-dead variant retains the ability to enhance catalytic activity of its co-receptor kinase BAK1/SERK3 (brassinosteroid insensitive 1-associated kinase 1/somatic embryogenesis receptor kinase 3).
evidence: This is a key finding from the study.

claim: The EFR kinase domain must adopt its active conformation in order to activate BAK1 allosterically.
source: Applying hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) analysis and designing homology-based intragenic suppressor mutations, we provide evidence that the EFR kinase domain must adopt its active conformation in order to activate BAK1 allosterically, likely by supporting αC-helix positioning in BAK1.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on HDX-MS data and mutational analysis.

claim: EFR likely activates BAK1 by supporting αC-helix positioning in BAK1.
source: Applying hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry (HDX-MS) analysis and designing homology-based intragenic suppressor mutations, we provide evidence that the EFR kinase domain must adopt its active conformation in order to activate BAK1 allosterically, likely by supporting αC-helix positioning in BAK1.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by the data.

claim: BAK1 first phosphorylates EFR in the activation loop to stabilize its active conformation.
source: Our results suggest a conformational toggle model for signaling, in which BAK1 first phosphorylates EFR in the activation loop to stabilize its active conformation, allowing EFR in turn to allosterically activate BAK1.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the study's findings.

claim: EFR allosterically activates BAK1 after being phosphorylated by BAK1.
source: Our results suggest a conformational toggle model for signaling, in which BAK1 first phosphorylates EFR in the activation loop to stabilize its active conformation, allowing EFR in turn to allosterically activate BAK1.
evidence: This is part of the proposed conformational toggle model.

claim: The G-protein coupled receptor family expanded in metazoans.
source: Whereas the G-protein coupled receptor family expanded in metazoans, the receptor kinase (RK) and receptor protein (RP) families expanded in plants (Shiu and Bleecker, 2003; Shiu and Bleecker, 2001; Trusov and Botella, 2016).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: The receptor kinase (RK) and receptor protein (RP) families expanded in plants.
source: Whereas the G-protein coupled receptor family expanded in metazoans, the receptor kinase (RK) and receptor protein (RP) families expanded in plants (Shiu and Bleecker, 2003; Shiu and Bleecker, 2001; Trusov and Botella, 2016).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Plant RKs resemble metazoan receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) in their organization.
source: Plant RKs resemble metazoan receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) in their organization, containing an extracellular ligand-sensing domain that is coupled to an intracellular kinase domain by a single-pass transmembrane helix (Hohmann et al., 2017; Lemmon and Schlessinger, 2010).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Plant RKs contain an extracellular ligand-sensing domain coupled to an intracellular kinase domain by a single-pass transmembrane helix.
source: Plant RKs resemble metazoan receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) in their organization, containing an extracellular ligand-sensing domain that is coupled to an intracellular kinase domain by a single-pass transmembrane helix (Hohmann et al., 2017; Lemmon and Schlessinger, 2010).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: The intracellular kinase domain of plant RKs is a serine/threonine kinase domain most closely related to IRAKs/Pelle kinases.
source: In contrast to RTKs, however, the intracellular kinase domain of plant RKs is a serine/threonine kinase domain most closely related to interleukin-1 receptor associated kinases (IRAKs)/Pelle kinases (Shiu and Bleecker, 2003; Shiu and Bleecker, 2001) – although dual-specificity kinase activity has been reported in some cases (Liu et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2020; Macho et al., 2014; Oh et al., 2009; Perraki et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Dual-specificity kinase activity has been reported in some plant RKs.
source: In contrast to RTKs, however, the intracellular kinase domain of plant RKs is a serine/threonine kinase domain most closely related to interleukin-1 receptor associated kinases (IRAKs)/Pelle kinases (Shiu and Bleecker, 2003; Shiu and Bleecker, 2001) – although dual-specificity kinase activity has been reported in some cases (Liu et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2020; Macho et al., 2014; Oh et al., 2009; Perraki et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: LRR-RKs are the most extensively studied sub-family of Arabidopsis thaliana RKs.
source: The leucine-rich repeat (LRR)-RKs are the most extensively studied sub-family of Arabidopsis thaliana (hereafter Arabidopsis) RKs.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the field.

claim: LRR-RKs primarily sense peptide ligands that regulate growth and development, or molecular patterns released during damage or microbial infection.
source: They primarily sense peptide ligands that regulate growth and development, or molecular patterns that are released during damage or microbial infection (Couto and Zipfel, 2016).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Ligand-binding LRR-RKs have long ectodomains (>20 LRRs).
source: Ligand-binding LRR-RKs have long ectodomains (>20 LRRs), and recruit short LRR ectodomain-containing co-receptor kinases (coRKs) upon ligand perception (Bender and Zipfel, 2023; Hohmann et al., 2017), most of which belong to the SERK (somatic embryogenesis receptor kinase) family.
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: LRR-RKs recruit short LRR ectodomain-containing co-receptor kinases (coRKs) upon ligand perception.
source: Ligand-binding LRR-RKs have long ectodomains (>20 LRRs), and recruit short LRR ectodomain-containing co-receptor kinases (coRKs) upon ligand perception (Bender and Zipfel, 2023; Hohmann et al., 2017), most of which belong to the SERK (somatic embryogenesis receptor kinase) family.
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Most coRKs recruited by LRR-RKs belong to the SERK family.
source: Ligand-binding LRR-RKs have long ectodomains (>20 LRRs), and recruit short LRR ectodomain-containing co-receptor kinases (coRKs) upon ligand perception (Bender and Zipfel, 2023; Hohmann et al., 2017), most of which belong to the SERK (somatic embryogenesis receptor kinase) family.
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: BRI1 is one of the most well characterized LRR-RKs.
source: One of the most well characterized LRR-RKs is BRI1 (brassinosteroid insensitive 1), which recruits the coRKs SERK1 and SERK3/BAK1 (BRI1-associated kinase 1) upon brassinosteroid (BR) perception (Albrecht et al., 2008; He et al., 2000; Hothorn et al., 2011; Nam and Li, 2002; Santiago et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: BRI1 recruits SERK1 and BAK1 upon brassinosteroid perception.
source: One of the most well characterized LRR-RKs is BRI1 (brassinosteroid insensitive 1), which recruits the coRKs SERK1 and SERK3/BAK1 (BRI1-associated kinase 1) upon brassinosteroid (BR) perception (Albrecht et al., 2008; He et al., 2000; Hothorn et al., 2011; Nam and Li, 2002; Santiago et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: The intracellular kinase domains of BRI1 and BAK1 reciprocally trans-phosphorylate each other in their activation loops after ligand perception.
source: After ligand perception, the intracellular kinase domains of BRI1 and BAK1 reciprocally trans-phosphorylate each other in their activation loops (Hohmann et al., 2017), and BAK1 then phosphorylates BRI1 in its juxtamembrane segment and C-tail to propagate BR signaling (Wang et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: BAK1 phosphorylates BRI1 in its juxtamembrane segment and C-tail to propagate BR signaling.
source: After ligand perception, the intracellular kinase domains of BRI1 and BAK1 reciprocally trans-phosphorylate each other in their activation loops (Hohmann et al., 2017), and BAK1 then phosphorylates BRI1 in its juxtamembrane segment and C-tail to propagate BR signaling (Wang et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: BRI1 exemplifies a set of BAK1-dependent LRR-RKs that have RD-type intracellular kinase domains and require their catalytic activity to signal.
source: BRI1 exemplifies a set of BAK1-dependent LRR-RKs that have RD-type intracellular kinase domains and require their catalytic activity to signal (Cao et al., 2013; Kosentka et al., 2017; Taylor et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: EFR has a non-RD intracellular kinase.
source: Other LRR-RKs such as EFR (elongation factor Tu receptor) instead have non-RD intracellular kinases, and are thought not to trans-phosphorylate their associated coRK following ligand perception (Schwessinger et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: EFR is thought not to trans-phosphorylate its associated coRK following ligand perception.
source: Other LRR-RKs such as EFR (elongation factor Tu receptor) instead have non-RD intracellular kinases, and are thought not to trans-phosphorylate their associated coRK following ligand perception (Schwessinger et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Kinase inactive mutants of EFR (D849N or K851E) retain signaling function.
source: Moreover, kinase inactive mutants of EFR (D849N or K851E) retain signaling function, a result that challenges the generality of the reciprocal trans-phosphorylation model (Bender et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: EFR perceives the pathogen-associated molecular pattern (PAMP) elongation factor Tu.
source: EFR perceives the pathogen-associated molecular pattern (PAMP) elongation factor Tu, or its active peptide epitope elf18 (Zipfel et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: EFR perceives the active peptide epitope elf18.
source: EFR perceives the pathogen-associated molecular pattern (PAMP) elongation factor Tu, or its active peptide epitope elf18 (Zipfel et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: PAMP perception by EFR triggers heterodimerization with BAK1.
source: PAMP perception triggers heterodimerization with the coRK BAK1, resulting in phosphorylation of the EFR intracellular kinase domain (Bender et al., 2021; Roux et al., 2011; Schulze et al., 2010; Schwessinger et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Heterodimerization of EFR with BAK1 results in phosphorylation of the EFR intracellular kinase domain.
source: PAMP perception triggers heterodimerization with the coRK BAK1, resulting in phosphorylation of the EFR intracellular kinase domain (Bender et al., 2021; Roux et al., 2011; Schulze et al., 2010; Schwessinger et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: The signal from EFR is relayed to the cytoplasmic kinases BIK1 and PBL1.
source: The signal is subsequently relayed to the cytoplasmic kinases BIK1 (botrytis-induced kinase 1) and PBL1 (PBS1-like 1) (Li et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2010; Ranf et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Immune signaling activation by EFR elicits an apoplastic oxidative burst.
source: The resulting immune signaling activation elicits a battery of cellular responses, including an apoplastic oxidative burst (hereafter oxidative burst), Ca2+-influx, callose deposition, MAPK (mitogen activated protein kinase) activation, and transcriptional reprogramming (DeFalco and Zipfel, 2021).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Immune signaling activation by EFR elicits Ca2+-influx.
source: The resulting immune signaling activation elicits a battery of cellular responses, including an apoplastic oxidative burst (hereafter oxidative burst), Ca2+-influx, callose deposition, MAPK (mitogen activated protein kinase) activation, and transcriptional reprogramming (DeFalco and Zipfel, 2021).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Immune signaling activation by EFR elicits callose deposition.
source: The resulting immune signaling activation elicits a battery of cellular responses, including an apoplastic oxidative burst (hereafter oxidative burst), Ca2+-influx, callose deposition, MAPK (mitogen activated protein kinase) activation, and transcriptional reprogramming (DeFalco and Zipfel, 2021).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Immune signaling activation by EFR elicits MAPK activation.
source: The resulting immune signaling activation elicits a battery of cellular responses, including an apoplastic oxidative burst (hereafter oxidative burst), Ca2+-influx, callose deposition, MAPK (mitogen activated protein kinase) activation, and transcriptional reprogramming (DeFalco and Zipfel, 2021).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Immune signaling activation by EFR elicits transcriptional reprogramming.
source: The resulting immune signaling activation elicits a battery of cellular responses, including an apoplastic oxidative burst (hereafter oxidative burst), Ca2+-influx, callose deposition, MAPK (mitogen activated protein kinase) activation, and transcriptional reprogramming (DeFalco and Zipfel, 2021).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Initial in vitro studies identified phosphorylation sites in EFR that result from auto-phosphorylation or trans-phosphorylation by BAK1.
source: Initial studies in vitro identified phosphorylation sites in EFR that result either from auto-phosphorylation or from trans-phosphorylation by BAK1 (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: In vivo phosphorylation sites on EFR were identified by immunoprecipitating EFR-GFP from elf18-treated seedlings.
source: More recently, in vivo phosphorylation sites on EFR were identified by immunoprecipitating EFR-GFP from elf18-treated seedlings (Bender et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: S888 in the EFR activation loop is phosphorylated in vitro and in vivo.
source: One was a serine (S888) in the activation loop (A-loop), at which phosphorylation was consistently observed in vitro and in vivo (Bender et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Ligand-inducible phosphorylation in the A-loop (S887/S888) of EFR is indispensable for signaling.
source: Despite the non-RD nature of EFR, and its ability to signal independently of catalytic activity, ligand-inducible phosphorylation in the A-loop (S887/S888) surprisingly proved indispensable for signaling (Bender et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Y836 in EFR is phosphorylated after ligand treatment in vivo.
source: Furthermore, a functionally important tyrosine in EFR (Y836) – conserved in subdomain VIa of many eukaryotic protein kinases (Lai et al., 2016; Luo et al., 2020; Perraki et al., 2018) – was found to be phosphorylated after ligand treatment in vivo (Macho et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: A phospho-ablative Y836F mutation in EFR blocks immune signaling.
source: A phospho-ablative Y836F mutation in EFR blocks immune signaling and resistance against the phytopathogenic bacterium Pseudomonas syringae (Macho et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: A phospho-ablative Y836F mutation in EFR blocks resistance against Pseudomonas syringae.
source: A phospho-ablative Y836F mutation in EFR blocks immune signaling and resistance against the phytopathogenic bacterium Pseudomonas syringae (Macho et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Adding rapamycin induced formation of FKBP-EFR/FRB-BAK1 dimers in size exclusion chromatography experiments.
source: We first confirmed that adding Rap induced formation of FKBP-EFR/FRB-BAK1 dimers in size exclusion chromatography experiments (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Rap addition increased BIK1D202N phosphorylation when the BRI1 kinase domain was dimerized with BAK1.
source: Rap addition increased BIK1D202N phosphorylation when the BRI1 or EFR kinase domains were dimerized with BAK1 (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Rap addition increased BIK1D202N phosphorylation when the EFR kinase domain was dimerized with BAK1.
source: Rap addition increased BIK1D202N phosphorylation when the BRI1 or EFR kinase domains were dimerized with BAK1 (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: EFR enhances BAK1 autophosphorylation activity.
source: The same trend was observed for phosphorylation of the BAK1 kinase domain itself, indicating that EFR also enhances BAK1 autophosphorylation activity (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: BIK1D202N did not co-elute with the EFR-BAK1 complex in size exclusion studies.
source: We found that BIK1D202N did not co-elute with the EFR-BAK1 complex in size exclusion studies, indicating that stable EFR/BAK1/BIK1 trimers do not form in vitro (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Stable EFR/BAK1/BIK1 trimers do not form in vitro.
source: We found that BIK1D202N did not co-elute with the EFR-BAK1 complex in size exclusion studies, indicating that stable EFR/BAK1/BIK1 trimers do not form in vitro (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: EFR increases BIK1 phosphorylation by allosterically activating the BAK1 kinase domain.
source: Our findings therefore support the hypothesis that EFR increases BIK1 phosphorylation by allosterically activating the BAK1 kinase domain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: EFR must be phosphorylated at S887/S888 in the A-loop to signal in vivo.
source: Although EFR's catalytic activity is dispensable for this effect – and for immune signaling – EFR must be phosphorylated at S887/S888 in the A-loop and Y836 to signal in vivo (Bender et al., 2021; Macho et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: EFR must be phosphorylated at Y836 to signal in vivo.
source: Although EFR's catalytic activity is dispensable for this effect – and for immune signaling – EFR must be phosphorylated at S887/S888 in the A-loop and Y836 to signal in vivo (Bender et al., 2021; Macho et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: EFRSSAA fails to activate the RK/coRK complex.
source: The phospho-ablative EFR A-loop mutant EFRSSAA fails to activate the RK/coRK complex, as ligand-induced phosphorylation of BAK1 S612 – a mark for active BAK1-containing receptor complexes (Perraki et al., 2018) – is obstructed despite retaining the ability to associate with BAK1 in a ligand-dependent manner (Bender et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: EFRSSAA retains the ability to associate with BAK1 in a ligand-dependent manner.
source: The phospho-ablative EFR A-loop mutant EFRSSAA fails to activate the RK/coRK complex, as ligand-induced phosphorylation of BAK1 S612 – a mark for active BAK1-containing receptor complexes (Perraki et al., 2018) – is obstructed despite retaining the ability to associate with BAK1 in a ligand-dependent manner (Bender et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: EFRY836F obstructed the induction of BAK1 S612 phosphorylation.
source: EFRY836F also obstructed the induction of BAK1 S612 phosphorylation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that EFRY836F and EFRSSAA impair receptor complex activation.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: EFRY836F and EFRSSAA impair receptor complex activation.
source: EFRY836F also obstructed the induction of BAK1 S612 phosphorylation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that EFRY836F and EFRSSAA impair receptor complex activation.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Y836 in EFR corresponds in sequence and structural alignments with Y156 in PKA.
source: Y836 in EFR corresponds in sequence and structural alignments with Y156 in the canonical kinase PKA (protein kinase A) (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2A), which is conserved in many protein kinases.
evidence: This is based on sequence and structural alignments shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2A.

claim: Y156 in PKA is conserved in many protein kinases.
source: Y836 in EFR corresponds in sequence and structural alignments with Y156 in the canonical kinase PKA (protein kinase A) (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2A), which is conserved in many protein kinases.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: One region is stabilized in EFRY836F compared to wild-type EFR.
source: Plotting differential HDX (Δ%EX) between unphosphorylated EFR and EFRY836F (aa684-1031) identifies one region that is stabilized in EFRY836F compared to wild-type and two that are destabilized (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from HDX-MS data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Two regions are destabilized in EFRY836F compared to wild-type EFR.
source: Plotting differential HDX (Δ%EX) between unphosphorylated EFR and EFRY836F (aa684-1031) identifies one region that is stabilized in EFRY836F compared to wild-type and two that are destabilized (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from HDX-MS data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The region stabilized in EFRY836F contains the N-terminal part of the A-loop.
source: The region stabilized in EFRY836F contains the N-terminal part of the A-loop, implying that this region makes more extensive contacts with the kinase core than in the unphosphorylated wild-type kinase domain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the HDX-MS data.

claim: The two regions that become more structurally flexible in EFRY836F include the β3-αC loop and the catalytic loop plus C-terminal end of the αE-helix.
source: The two regions that become more structurally flexible in EFRY836F include the β3-αC loop and the catalytic loop plus C-terminal end of the αE-helix – where Y836 is located (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is a direct observation from HDX-MS data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Y836 is important in regulating kinase domain allosteric transitions.
source: Because these two regions are both important for conformational switching, the HDX-MS results suggest that Y836 is important in regulating kinase domain allosteric transitions.
evidence: This is an inference from the HDX-MS data.

claim: The side-chain of Y836 forms hydrogen-bonds with the αC-β4 loop backbone in active kinase conformations.
source: Consistent with this, crystal structures as well as AlphaFold2 models of active kinase conformations (Faezov and Dunbrack, 2023) suggest that the side-chain of this tyrosine forms hydrogen-bonds (H-bond) with the αC-β4 loop backbone to establish an inter-lobe connection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of the inter-lobe connection may underlie the observed alterations in EFRY836F conformational dynamics.
source: Loss of this inter-lobe connection may underlie the observed alterations in EFRY836F conformational dynamics in EFRY836F, resulting from inaccessibility of the active-like conformation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural and HDX-MS data.

claim: The F761H mutation partially restored oxidative bursts of EFRY836F.
source: EFR F761H partially restored oxidative bursts of EFRY836F and EFRSSAA. Outliers are in indicated by asterisk in addition to the outlier itself and are included in statistical analysis; Statistical test: Kruskal-Wallis test (p<2.2*10–16 in C, p=1.163*10–7 in D), Dunn's post-hoc test with Benjamin-Hochberg correction (p ≤ 0.05) Groups with like lowercase letter designations are not statistically different.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The F761H mutation partially restored oxidative bursts of EFRSSAA.
source: EFR F761H partially restored oxidative bursts of EFRY836F and EFRSSAA. Outliers are in indicated by asterisk in addition to the outlier itself and are included in statistical analysis; Statistical test: Kruskal-Wallis test (p<2.2*10–16 in C, p=1.163*10–7 in D), Dunn's post-hoc test with Benjamin-Hochberg correction (p ≤ 0.05) Groups with like lowercase letter designations are not statistically different.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Only EFRF761[H/M] could functionally recover EFRY836F as the oxidative burst was partially restored.
source: Only EFRF761[H/M] could functionally recover EFRY836F as the oxidative burst was partially restored.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: EFRL873E showed a WT-like oxidative burst.
source: EFRL873E showed a WT-like oxidative burst but EFRL873E/Y836F did not restore the oxidative burst.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: EFRL873E/Y836F did not restore the oxidative burst.
source: EFRL873E showed a WT-like oxidative burst but EFRL873E/Y836F did not restore the oxidative burst.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The F761H mutation restores EFRSSAA function.
source: Our finding that the F761H mutation restores EFRSSAA function further supports this hypothesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data.

claim: Two independent homozygous complementation lines were isolated for EFRF761H/Y836F and EFRF761H/SSAA.
source: Two independent homozygous complementation lines were isolated, with similar accumulation of EFR-GFP protein in the T3 generation.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claim: The oxidative burst was partially restored in stable Arabidopsis complementation lines that express EFRF761H/Y836F.
source: Similar to experiments in N. benthamiana, the oxidative burst was partially restored in stable Arabidopsis complementation lines that express EFRF761H/Y836F or EFRF761H/SSAA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The oxidative burst was partially restored in stable Arabidopsis complementation lines that express EFRF761H/SSAA.
source: Similar to experiments in N. benthamiana, the oxidative burst was partially restored in stable Arabidopsis complementation lines that express EFRF761H/Y836F or EFRF761H/SSAA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: EFRF761H/Y836F and EFRF761H/SSAA complementation lines exhibited enhanced seedling growth inhibition compared to EFRY836F and EFRSSAA, respectively.
source: As expected, both independent complementation lines of EFRF761H/Y836F and EFRF761H/SSAA exhibited enhanced SGI compared to EFRY836F and EFRSSAA, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MAPK activation was abolished or severely impaired in both EFRY836F and EFRSSAA complementation lines.
source: We also observed that MAPK activation was abolished or severely impaired in both EFRY836F and EFRSSAA complementation lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) and recovered in EFRF761H/Y836F and EFRF761H/SSAA complementation lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: MAPK activation was recovered in EFRF761H/Y836F and EFRF761H/SSAA complementation lines.
source: We also observed that MAPK activation was abolished or severely impaired in both EFRY836F and EFRSSAA complementation lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) and recovered in EFRF761H/Y836F and EFRF761H/SSAA complementation lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Infection by Agrobacterium tumefaciens is restricted in Arabidopsis by EFR.
source: Infection by this bacterium is restricted in Arabidopsis by EFR, so loss-of-function mutants like efr-1 are more susceptible (Zipfel et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Loss-of-function mutants like efr-1 are more susceptible to Agrobacterium tumefaciens.
source: Infection by this bacterium is restricted in Arabidopsis by EFR, so loss-of-function mutants like efr-1 are more susceptible (Zipfel et al., 2006).
